title: One-time genomic cure of severe monogenic skin disease through the epidermal stem-cell compartment

concept.text: The proposed innovation is a one-time genetic treatment that restores function in diseased skin by correcting enough of the long-lived epidermal stem cells that continually renew it. Their descendants would retain the restored function as older surface cells are shed. The intended result is sustained benefit in treated tissue without repeated corrective treatment. Durable local restoration already has clinical precedent; the broader capability would make that outcome reliable across different disease genes and more difficult tissue settings.

Genetic correction can take different forms. Integrating gene replacement adds a functional gene to stem cells, whereas precise editing changes a disease-causing sequence or introduces corrective DNA at a targeted location. Both could satisfy this concept if they produce durable, functional stem-cell populations with acceptable safety. Ex vivo treatment corrects cells outside the body before transplanting epidermal sheets; future in vivo approaches would need to reach and correct the relevant stem cells within the patient. Precise editing is therefore a possible route, rather than a mandatory feature of every qualifying treatment.

Scope synthesis: the proposed advance extends beyond a successful graft for one epidermolysis bullosa subtype. It seeks convincing results across distinct causal genes and includes restoration at a difficult site, such as mucosa or intact but malfunctioning epidermis. Severe ichthyoses and xeroderma pigmentosum are proposed applications; the supplied clinical evidence concerns epidermolysis bullosa. The concept does not require a single vector for every mutation, and it does not include using corrected skin as a factory for systemic drugs.

significance.text: Severe epidermolysis bullosa causes persistent skin fragility, wounds and extracutaneous disease. Correcting the regenerative source of the epidermis could sustain local tissue function despite continual cell turnover, reducing dependence on repeated corrective gene delivery. The revolutionary extension would be reliable, reproducible restoration across diseases and tissue settings, building on the substantial local benefits already demonstrated by stem-cell grafting.

Benefits at mucosal or intact-skin sites remain conditional on successful delivery, stem-cell correction or engraftment, and persistence at those sites. In particular, the February 2026 review identifies inaccessible mucosa, including the esophagus and gastrointestinal tract, as a major unresolved target. Systemic delivery might eventually expand treatment reach, but the review treats delivery to internal tissues as a development requirement, not an established substitute for local grafting.

Impact synthesis: sustained function in treated skin would not by itself establish whole-body correction, elimination of extracutaneous disease, or freedom from all subsequent care. Successful treatment of two diseases would demonstrate broader applicability, not universal mutation coverage. Nor would it establish zero genomic risk. Extension to ichthyoses or xeroderma pigmentosum could be consequential, but the supplied EB-focused evidence does not establish those diseases' current treatment status or demonstrate their correction.

missing_breakthrough.text: The central unsolved capability is reliable correction of enough long-lived, regenerative epidermal stem cells across distinct disease genes and tissue settings. Correcting short-lived cells alone cannot establish a persistently corrected epidermis. Koller's 2023 editorial offers an insufficient number of corrected epidermal stem cells as a possible explanation for limited maintenance in some earlier recessive dystrophic epidermolysis bullosa graft studies. That is a hypothesis about particular outcomes, rather than proof that inadequate correction of holoclones explains every graft failure.

Delivery and tissue occupation remain separate engineering barriers. Non-integrating topical B-VEC requires repeated application; integrating stem-cell grafts can provide durable local benefit but require cell preparation and transplantation. The February 2026 review describes EB genome editing as predominantly ex vivo and preclinical, and reports that genetic correction of inaccessible gastrointestinal and esophageal mucosa had not been demonstrated. Proposed extension to intact malfunctioning epidermis adds a further requirement: corrected stem cells must become established and persist in that setting. The supplied evidence does not establish a general quantitative comparison of its difficulty with open-wound grafting.

Genomic safety and consistency across causal genes also remain barriers. Editing can produce unintended changes at the intended target as well as elsewhere in the genome, while integrating vectors require assessment of insertion-related risks. The 2026 review describes variable efficacy between loci and the potential cost and time required for mutation-specific therapies. Emerging whole-gene integration approaches may broaden treatment within certain subtypes, but they do not establish one universally applicable correction method.

Remaining uncertainty: immune responses to a restored protein are a relevant question for extending treatment across genodermatoses, but the supplied texts do not establish their general frequency, severity or unresolved status across such a platform. This concern should remain an explicit subject for investigation rather than a categorical claim that restored-protein immunity prevents durable correction.

current_state.text: The supplied research identifies Hirsch and colleagues' 2017 LAMB3 junctional epidermolysis bullosa case as a major demonstration of extensive epidermal regeneration. Koller's June 2023 editorial describes retroviral transgenic epidermal stem-cell grafts covering approximately 80% of a child's body surface area over three surgeries, and reports effectiveness eight years after treatment. These details are retained as the editorial's account, as characterized by the supplied review; the underlying Nature report was not independently inspected in that review. The result establishes an important local regenerative capability in a particular disease setting, rather than reproducibility across multiple causal genes or tissue types.

Historical limitations in recessive dystrophic epidermolysis bullosa graft maintenance should be read alongside later long-term benefit. The February 2026 review reports that, after a mean follow-up of 5.9 years, 70% of treated sites across seven RDEB patients showed at least 50% wound healing. This is substantial evidence of durable local benefit. It is neither evidence of complete healing at every site nor a demonstration of whole-body correction, but it prevents earlier graft limitations from being mistaken for the current limit of the entire approach.

Vyjuvek, beremagene geperpavec or B-VEC, is an approved topical HSV-1 therapy that delivers COL7A1. Koller's 2023 editorial summarizes complete wound healing as 67% with B-VEC versus 22% with placebo at six months. The February 2026 review separately reports B-VEC wound closure of 71% at three months and 67% at six months. Those time-point percentages should not be converted into a claim that an identical 67% of wounds healed by month three and continuously remained healed through month six. The supplied summaries do not provide the wound-level evidence needed for that interpretation. B-VEC requires repeated application and does not permanently correct the epidermal stem-cell compartment.

Stanford's June 23, 2025 news release reports FDA approval on April 29, 2025 of its gene-corrected RDEB graft therapy, identifies the VIITAL publication as prademagene zamikeracel, and describes results in 11 patients with 43 wound pairs. At week 24, at least 50% healing occurred in 81% of treated wounds versus 16% of control wounds; complete healing occurred in 16% versus none. The February 2026 review identifies the approved therapy as Zevaskyn. These results concern locally applied epidermal sheets for chronic wounds and do not demonstrate mucosal or whole-body correction.

The VIITAL figures above come from the retained Stanford news release, not direct inspection of the trial paper. The supplied Lancet abstract URL was not captured. Earlier notes gave exact counts of 35 of 43 treated wounds and 7 of 43 controls reaching at least half healing; those counts are consistent with the reported rounded percentages but were not directly printed in the retained texts described by the review. The percentages and denominator are therefore the supported quantitative account here, while the exact counts remain unverified in this record.

The February 2026 CRISPR review was available in full HTML and PDF according to the supplied evidence review, correcting the earlier characterization of abstract-only access. Its broad statement about the absence of a permanent treatment must be interpreted alongside documented durable local graft benefits: the remaining gap is a broadly applicable cure, not the absence of any lasting correction. It documents continuing delivery, stem-cell targeting and genomic-safety barriers. The supplied record does not establish comprehensive coverage of developments after February 2026 through November 1, 2026; the later source-retrieval date alone does not resolve that gap.

completion_criteria.text: Proposed demonstration: a single corrective intervention, ex vivo or in vivo, would produce at least three years of stable restored function without further corrective treatment in treated tissue for two severe genodermatoses involving different causal genes. Molecular evidence would show that corrected epidermal stem-cell clones persist and continue to supply functional tissue. At least one demonstration would include mucosa or an intact-skin disease such as a severe ichthyosis. These are proposed evaluative thresholds, not established clinical or regulatory standards.
completion_criteria.label: Single intervention restores three-year function across two genetically distinct genodermatoses

completion_criteria.text: Proposed reproducibility and functional evidence: results should recur in independent patients and separately prepared treatments, with transparent reporting of the treated area, causal variants, successful and failed sites, and the functional outcome relevant to each disease. Persistent corrective DNA or protein expression alone would be insufficient without sustained tissue function. Follow-up should distinguish renewed corrective treatment from other supportive care. A successful single junctional EB graft and repeatedly dosed wound therapy remain important achieved components, but would not complete this broader demonstration.
completion_criteria.label: Sustained tissue function recurs across independent patients and treatment preparations

completion_criteria.text: Proposed safety evidence: assessment should match the intervention and include unintended on-target and off-target changes for editing, insertion-related risks for integrating vectors, and longitudinal evidence about the behavior of corrected clones. Delivery complications and clinically relevant responses to treatment or restored protein should also be evaluated. These proposed assessments respond to documented genomic and delivery concerns; the supplied evidence does not establish a universal numerical threshold for acceptable risk.
completion_criteria.label: Intervention-specific genomic risks, clonal behavior and clinical safety are assessed

completion_criteria.text: Interpretive boundary of the proposal: three years would establish durability over that interval, not lifelong cure. Success across two causal genes and selected tissue sites would establish demonstrated breadth, not literal universality. Claims should remain bounded by the treated area and tissue type, the patients studied, follow-up duration and the genomic risks the measurements can detect. Whole-body benefit, extracutaneous correction and further disease applications would each require additional evidence.
completion_criteria.label: Claims remain bounded by demonstrated durability, breadth and detectable risks

related_concepts.text: Roster-based synthesis — DER-01, Clinical restoration of a complete human skin organ: both concepts involve regenerative cells and tissue engineering. DER-02 focuses on durable genetic restoration through the epidermal stem-cell compartment; that does not by itself establish restoration of a complete skin organ with all its structures and functions.

Roster-based synthesis — DER-04, Programmable passage of macromolecules and gene editors across intact stratum corneum: improved passage could enable an in vivo route for DER-02. Crossing the surface barrier would still leave stem-cell targeting, sufficient correction, persistence and genomic safety to demonstrate. DER-02 could also succeed through ex vivo grafting without solving intact-skin delivery.

Roster-based synthesis — DER-05, Epidermal DNA repair sufficient to prevent ultraviolet-driven skin cancer, and DER-06, Therapeutic reset of the mutant epidermal field: these overlap with DER-02 in durable changes to epidermal cell populations. DER-05 targets prevention of ultraviolet-driven cancer, while DER-06 targets an established mutant field. A proposed xeroderma pigmentosum application could connect DER-02 with DER-05, but correcting an inherited defect would not automatically establish cancer prevention or removal of pre-existing mutant clones.

Roster-based synthesis — DER-03, Antigen-selective erasure of pathogenic cutaneous immune memory, and DER-07, A skin-origin intervention that prevents atopic dermatitis and the atopic march: these address immune memory or prevention of an inflammatory disease trajectory. DER-02 instead addresses inherited defects through genetically corrected epidermal stem cells. Improved local skin function would not by itself demonstrate either selective immune-memory erasure or prevention of the atopic march.

Roster-based synthesis — DER-08, Reconstitution of melanocyte stem cells where the follicular reservoir is gone: both depend on establishing a durable regenerative cell population, but they target different compartments. Persistent corrected epidermal stem cells do not establish that a lost melanocyte stem-cell reservoir has been rebuilt.

Roster-based synthesis — DER-09, Durable regenerative closure of diabetic foot ulcers after ischemia and pressure are treated, and DER-10, In situ reversal of established keloids and pathological cutaneous scars: all three concern durable tissue improvement, but their causal targets differ. DER-02 corrects an inherited epidermal defect; DER-09 addresses ulcer regeneration after vascular and mechanical contributors are treated; DER-10 addresses established pathological scarring. EB wound-healing results cannot establish either diabetic-ulcer regeneration or scar reversal.

unresolved_issues: Comprehensive coverage of developments after February 2026 through November 1, 2026 is not established by the supplied freshness record.
The exact VIITAL counts of 35 of 43 treated wounds and 7 of 43 controls remain unverified in the retained texts; the underlying Lancet artifact was not captured.

The attribution and chronology of the eight-year follow-up warrant clarification: the supplied materials associate that duration with Koller's account of the child graft case while also identifying the landmark report as published in 2017. The editorial's reported duration is preserved without an invented resolution.
The supplied B-VEC summaries do not resolve wound-level continuity between the three-month and six-month outcomes.
The evidence does not establish correction of inaccessible gastrointestinal or esophageal mucosa, or the proposed intact-skin extension.
Restored-protein immunity across genodermatoses and clinical extension to severe ichthyoses or xeroderma pigmentosum are not established by these EB-focused sources.

The three-year, two-causal-gene and difficult-site thresholds are proposals; the supplied evidence does not establish a consensus threshold or the patient numbers needed to demonstrate reproducibility.

brief.title: Lasting repair for inherited skin disease
possible: People born with severe inherited skin disease could receive a single genetic treatment that keeps treated skin functioning as it renews itself. The treatment would correct stem cells, the long-lived cells that continually replace the skin’s surface.

Corrected cells could be grown into skin sheets and transplanted, or eventually treated inside the body. The goal is reliable repair across diseases caused by different genes, including hard-to-treat internal linings or skin that remains intact but functions poorly.
why: For people whose skin blisters and wounds under slight friction, lasting repair could reduce painful wounds and the daily burden of care. Correcting the cells that renew skin could also reduce dependence on repeated genetic treatment.

sources.showed: Koller reviewed clinical gene treatments for epidermolysis bullosa, an inherited blistering disease. Genetically corrected skin grafts provided lasting repair, while a gene-delivering gel improved wound healing with repeated application.
sources.quote: The transgenic epidermis is sustained by a defined number of regenerative epidermal stem cells, resulting in long-term clinical outcomes with no severe adverse effects reported to date.
sources.cited_for: Corrected stem cells can sustain functioning skin after transplantation.
sources.not_established: Reliable repair across different disease genes and difficult tissue sites remains to be demonstrated.

sources.who: Alex du Rand, Ben Buttle and Hilary Sheppard
sources.showed: Their review describes lasting local benefits from gene-corrected grafts and progress in gene editing, which changes DNA at chosen locations. Unintended DNA changes and delivery to the right cells remain barriers.
sources.quote:
We find that the widespread application
of Cas9 nuclease is currently hindered by off-target genotoxicity, which can be mitigated using Cas9 nickases.
sources.cited_for: Lasting local repair has clinical precedent, while gene editing still faces delivery and DNA-safety barriers.
sources.not_established: Broad clinical use still requires reliable correction of renewing cells and acceptable safety across disease genes.

sources.showed: This is a clinical trial of gene-corrected skin grafts for chronic wounds in recessive dystrophic epidermolysis bullosa, an inherited blistering disease.
sources.cited_for: Clinical testing of gene-corrected skin sheets for persistent wounds.
sources.not_established: The trial does not establish repair of internal linings or the whole body.

sources.who: Jean Tang and the Stanford Medicine-led trial team
sources.showed: In a trial involving 11 patients, wounds treated with genetically corrected skin grafts healed better and had less pain and itching than comparison wounds receiving usual care.
sources.quote: In addition, patients’ reports of pain, itching and blistering were better on the grafted areas than the control wounds, having shown more improvement from baseline.
sources.cited_for: Gene-corrected grafts can improve persistent wounds and symptoms in a small clinical trial.
sources.not_established: These local wound results leave long-term durability across other disease genes and tissue settings unresolved.

shown: Hirsch and colleagues regenerated skin using genetically corrected stem-cell grafts in a child with an inherited blistering disease. The grafts covered about 80% of the child’s body surface, demonstrating extensive local repair.

Stanford-led trials have also shown lasting wound-healing benefits from corrected skin sheets in another genetic form of the disease. The resulting graft therapy, Zevaskyn, has received approval for treating wounds.
missing: Reliable, lasting correction across diseases caused by different genes still needs demonstration.
Corrected stem cells must become established and persist in internal linings or intact, malfunctioning skin.
Treatment-specific DNA risks and the long-term behavior of corrected cell populations need assessment.

milestones.label: Lasting function across genetically distinct skin diseases
milestones.explanation: A single treatment would have to restore function for three years across distinct genetic diseases, including an internal lining or intact-skin disease. Persistent corrected stem cells would explain the lasting repair.

milestones.label: Independent patients and treatment preparations achieve sustained function
milestones.explanation: Lasting tissue function would have to recur across independent patients and separately prepared treatments, with successes and failures reported. This would establish reproducibility beyond isolated successes.

milestones.label: DNA changes and long-term treatment safety are assessed
milestones.explanation: Studies would have to assess unintended DNA changes, corrected cell populations over time, delivery complications and immune responses. These findings would establish the risks of each treatment approach.

milestones.label: Claims match demonstrated duration, reach and measured risks
milestones.explanation: Claims would have to reflect the treated tissues, patients, follow-up and risks the tests can detect. This would keep conclusions about durability and breadth within what the results establish.

uncertain: The proposed durability and disease-breadth thresholds lack consensus, and the patient numbers needed to establish reproducibility remain open.
How often would immune responses to a restored protein limit lasting repair across different inherited skin diseases?
Benefits in treated skin leave effects on disease elsewhere in the body unresolved.

page.title: One-time curative epidermal stem-cell gene therapy for inherited skin disease
page.definition: A patient's epidermal stem cells, the long-lived cells that renew the skin's outer layer, are genetically corrected once, in transplanted sheets or inside the body, so that treated tissue stays functional for years without repeat treatment. The capability holds for inherited skin diseases caused by different genes, and in mucosa or intact skin as well as open wounds.

goal.need: Wounds selected for VIITAL had remained open for 0.5–21 years. A preclinical junctional epidermolysis bullosa study estimated one epidermal renewal cycle at 3–4 weeks. The therapeutic objective is continued production of a missing adhesion protein by the stem cells that sustain transplanted epidermis.

statements.context: The passage states the trial's aim. Hologene 5 is a genetically modified epidermal graft for LAMB3-related junctional epidermolysis bullosa.

completion.title: A single stem-cell gene treatment keeps tissue functional for 3 years in two genetic skin diseases.
completion.criterion: One corrective treatment of epidermal stem cells, ex vivo or in vivo, keeps treated tissue healed and free of blistering, or meets the disease's own functional measure, for at least 3 years with no further corrective treatment, in each of two severe inherited skin diseases caused by different genes. Each disease needs at least 3 patients given separately manufactured treatments, with treated area and failed sites stated in a peer-reviewed or regulator's report. Molecular analysis at 3 years or later shows corrected stem-cell clones maintaining the tissue. In at least one disease the treated site is mucosa or intact skin, not an open skin wound. Repeatedly applied therapy does not count.
completion.set_by: Technology Atlas. The 3-year period, two causal genes, 3 patients per disease and the mucosal or intact-skin site come from this entry's record; no regulator or society defines when a one-time epidermal gene therapy counts as curative. The quoted review, published after ZEVASKYN was licensed, states that no permanent curative therapy exists.
completion.threshold_quote: In the absence of a permanent curative therapy for any EB subtype, treatment is palliative
completion.basis: The former test, a regulator's licence for a gene-modified epidermal graft in one genetic form of epidermolysis bullosa, is now milestone m4. That licence rests on wound healing and pain at 24 weeks and does not certify durable correction, a second causal gene or mucosal treatment. Three years establishes durability over that interval, not lifelong cure. Licensure is neither required nor sufficient. Whole-body correction and a single vector for every mutation are not asked for.

milestones.title: Corrected patient cells regenerate skin with the missing adhesion protein in an animal model.
milestones.criterion: Preclinical proof of concept demonstrates disease-relevant protein restoration and tissue regeneration in vivo, with biodistribution and toxicology supporting human dosing. LAMB3 junctional epidermolysis bullosa: cells from six unrelated patients regenerated skin with laminin-332 and hemidesmosomes on immunodeficient mice in 2001. COL7A1 recessive dystrophic epidermolysis bullosa: FDA-reviewed mouse grafts expressed collagen VII for up to 12 months with normal epidermal differentiation. These are observed results; the guidance specifies no common numerical correction threshold.
milestones.set_by: FDA, Human Gene Therapy for Rare Diseases, section IV; this is nonbinding preclinical guidance applicable across the cases.
milestones.threshold_quote: should demonstrate a biological response to the investigational GT product that is similar to the expected response in humans.

milestones.title: An epidermal gene therapy graft engrafts and restores its missing adhesion protein in people.
milestones.criterion: An authorised early-phase human study demonstrates graft engraftment and restoration of the disease-specific adhesion protein, with tissue function and safety assessed. In LAMB3 junctional epidermolysis bullosa, one 36-year-old man received nine grafts covering approximately 500 cm²; functional epidermis persisted for one year in the 2006 report. In COL7A1 recessive dystrophic epidermolysis bullosa, seven patients received grafts; three had detectable collagen VII NC2 domain or anchoring fibrils at one year.
milestones.set_by: Clinical proof-of-concept convention used in early-phase epidermal gene therapy: the Ministry-authorised Mavilio et al. JEB study and the FDA-reviewed RDEB phase 1/2a programme.
milestones.threshold_quote: Retroviral integration site analysis indicated that the regenerated epidermis is maintained by a defined repertoire of transduced stem cells.

milestones.title: An epidermal gene therapy graft improves wound healing and pain at 24 weeks in a controlled trial.
milestones.criterion: VIITAL compares grafts with matched control wounds for both ≥50% healing from baseline at 24 weeks, confirmed at least two weeks later, and pain reduction on the Wong-Baker FACES scale. Both comparisons must favour treatment statistically. Among 11 patients, 35/43 treated versus 7/43 control wounds reached the healing endpoint (p<0.0001); mean pain reductions were 3.07 versus 0.90 points (42 evaluable pairs; p=0.0002). For LAMB3 junctional epidermolysis bullosa, Hologene 5 ended early with two participants; its different 12-month primary endpoint was evaluable in neither, according to results posted on 17 April 2026.
milestones.set_by: FDA, ZEVASKYN Summary Basis for Regulatory Action, accepting VIITAL's co-primary efficacy endpoints. The 24-week tests were specified for COL7A1 RDEB and are not validated thresholds for LAMB3 JEB.
milestones.threshold_quote: The co-primary endpoints were wound healing and pain reduction at Week 24.

milestones.title: A regulator licenses a gene-modified epidermal graft for one genetic form of epidermolysis bullosa.
milestones.criterion: A regulator such as the FDA or the European Commission licenses autologous epidermal sheets, genetically modified outside the body to produce the deficient adhesion protein, for treating wounds in one genetically specified form of epidermolysis bullosa. Durability beyond the pivotal trial's endpoint, other causal genes and mucosal sites are not required. This was the entry's completion test until 16 November 2026.
milestones.set_by: FDA, biologics licence application 125807, approval letter for ZEVASKYN; the decision concerns recessive dystrophic epidermolysis bullosa. This is the former completion test.
milestones.threshold_quote: Under this license, you are authorized to manufacture the product prademagene zamikeracel

milestones.title: One graft treatment keeps skin functional for 3 years, sustained by corrected stem-cell clones.
milestones.criterion: In one severe inherited skin disease, a single application of genetically corrected epidermal grafts keeps the treated skin healed and free of blistering for at least 3 years with no further corrective treatment in at least one patient, in a peer-reviewed report. Integration-site or equivalent molecular analysis shows that corrected stem-cell clones maintain the regenerated epidermis. A second causal gene, mucosa and intact skin are not required.
milestones.set_by: Technology Atlas; the completion test's durability and clonal evidence without its breadth. The quoted editorial describes the junctional epidermolysis bullosa grafts in these terms; no outside body sets the period.
milestones.threshold_quote: The transgenic epidermis is sustained by a defined number of regenerative epidermal stem cells, resulting in long-term clinical outcomes with no severe adverse effects reported to date.

not_found: No externally set test combining a cross-genodermatosis cure, three years of durability, two causal genes and a mucosal or intact-skin result was located in regulatory, society or trial documents.
No common follow-up duration certifying lifelong correction was located.
The Lancet VIITAL page and the supplied EurekAlert page returned access errors.
The FDA summary did not disclose the number of mice underlying its reported preclinical graft-persistence results.

results.finding: In 11 patients contributing 43 wound pairs, 81% of grafted wounds versus 16% of controls were at least half healed at 24 weeks.
results.detail: The release reports significantly better healing and less pain, but does not specify confirmation at least two weeks later, the Wong-Baker FACES scale, or statistical results for both required comparisons.
results.quote: At 24 weeks after grafting, 81% of treated wounds were at least half healed, compared with 16% of control wounds.

results.finding: One autologous gene-modified epidermal graft therapy for recessive dystrophic EB received FDA approval on April 29, 2025.
results.detail: The release reports FDA approval and describes patient-derived skin sheets genetically corrected to produce collagen VII; it is not the regulator's decision record.
results.quote:
The skin grafts were
granted approval
as an EB therapy on April 29 by the U.S. Food and Drug Administration.

results.finding: Corrected keratinocytes from six JEB patients regenerated skin on SCID mice with laminin β3 expression lasting 8 weeks and restored hemidesmosomes.
results.detail: Demonstrates protein restoration and tissue regeneration in vivo, but reports no biodistribution or toxicology supporting human dosing. Approximately 15% of specimens were unanalyzable because of graft failure.
results.quote:
Tissue regenerated from β3-transduced JEB keratinocytes produced
 phenotypically normal skin characterized by sustained β3 expression
 and the formation of hemidesmosomes.

results.finding: Gene-modified human keratinocyte grafts in mice (sample size unstated) expressed collagen VII for up to 12 months.
results.detail: Grafts showed normal epidermal differentiation and collagen VII assembly. Biodistribution showed localization to grafts, with vector below detection in other tissues; toxicology found no gross or histopathological abnormalities.
results.quote:
RVV-transduced keratinocytes remained 
localized within explanted nonclinical products, and RVV-mediated expression of Col7 
was detected for up to 12-months post-implantation.

results.finding: In the seven-patient Phase 1/2a graft study, three patients had detectable collagen VII NC2 domain or anchoring fibrils at one year.
results.detail: The early-phase study assessed wound healing and safety, with greater healing in treated wounds than unmatched controls. Biopsies demonstrated restoration of the disease-specific adhesion protein.

results.finding: VIITAL enrolled 11 patients: 35/43 treated versus 7/43 control wounds achieved ≥50% healing at 24 weeks.
results.detail: Healing favoured treatment (p<0.0001), with success confirmed at least two weeks later. Wong-Baker FACES pain reductions were 3.07 versus 0.90 points across 42 evaluable pairs (p=0.0002).
results.quote:
At week 24, a 
higher proportion of ZEVASKYN treated wounds (81.4%) achieved ≥50% healing from 
baseline compared to control wounds (16.3%; p<0.0001).

results.finding: FDA's regulatory action summary records approval of one autologous gene-modified epidermal sheet product, ZEVASKYN, for RDEB wounds.
results.detail: The document explicitly identifies itself as the basis of approval. ZEVASKYN comprises autologous keratinocyte sheets genetically modified ex vivo to express COL7A1, for adult and pediatric RDEB wounds.
results.quote:
This document summarizes the basis of approval of ZEVASKYN for treatment of wounds 
in recessive dystrophic epidermolysis bullosa (RDEB).

results.finding: One patient's engrafted epidermis expressed normal laminin-332 and remained functional at 6.5 years.
results.detail: Follow-up of an authorised phase I/II trial demonstrated restored epidermal adhesion and normal hemidesmosomes. No tumors or evidence of clonal expansion were observed.
results.quote:
In contrast, control and trans-
genic epidermis expressed virtually identical amounts
of laminin 332- b3, which was properly located at the
epidermal-dermal junction ( Figures 2 A and 2B).

results.finding: One patient's genetically corrected grafts maintained functional, blister-free skin for 6.5 years, sustained by corrected epidermal stem cells.
results.detail: Follow-up after the original graft treatment reports no further corrective treatment. Integration-site analysis of late biopsies identified six independent integrations supporting maintenance by long-lived corrected stem-cell clones; blisters persisted outside the grafts.
results.quote:
During the 6.5-year follow-up, the epidermis of both of
Claudio’s upper legs was normal looking, normally pig-
mented, and robust, and did not itch or form blisters, either
spontaneously or after induced mechanical stress (such as
biopsy withdrawal).

results.finding: Follow-up of two previously grafted LAMB3-JEB patients reports functional transgenic epidermis lasting up to 16 years.
results.detail: The source adds long-term observations, including blister-free functional skin in the pediatric patient. It does not report integration-site or equivalent molecular analysis demonstrating maintenance by corrected stem-cell clones; that mechanism is reviewed from earlier work.
results.quote: An ongoing observational study confirms both the stability of the transgenic epidermis and the absence of AEs 16years after transplantation.

results.finding: Among 7 graft recipients, 3 had detectable C7 NC2 domain or anchoring fibrils at 12 months.
results.detail: FDA- and IRB-approved phase 1/2a study demonstrated graft healing and protein restoration, assessed tissue function and safety, and reported no serious related adverse events.
results.quote: At 12 months, 3 out of 7 participants were positive for either NC2 or AFs, indicating restoration of C7

results.finding: In 7 participants, ≥50% healing at 6 months occurred in 36/38 treated wounds versus 0/6 controls.
results.detail: Healing significantly favored treatment (P<0.0001), but this was not VIITAL. Pain was assessed as present or absent, without the required controlled Wong-Baker FACES comparison; endpoint confirmation at least two weeks later was not reported.
results.quote:
Wound healing of 50% or greater by IGA was present in 95% (36 of 38) of treated wounds versus 0% (0 of 6) of untreated control wounds at 6 months (
P
< 0.0001).

results.finding: In the 7-participant cohort, 16/20 assessed treated sites retained ≥50% healing at 3 years.
results.detail: Three-year wound improvement does not establish continuously healed, blister-free skin. No integration-site or equivalent analysis demonstrated maintenance by corrected stem-cell clones; molecular protein assessments extended only to 2 years.
results.quote: Importantly, the majority of treated sites continued to remain at least 50% healed at 2 years (71%) and 3 years (80%) after treatment.

results.finding: In seven adults receiving EB-101, 39/42 grafted sites achieved ≥50% wound healing at six months.
results.detail: This nonrandomized Phase 1/2a study lacks the required paired, controlled healing and Wong-Baker FACES pain comparisons at 24 weeks and subsequent healing confirmation. Systematic comparisons of treated and control wounds could not be performed.
results.quote:
Six months after 
application, 92.9% (39/42) of grafted sites achieved ≥ 50% 
wound healing.

results.finding: In seven adults receiving EB-101, 21/30 assessed treated sites showed ≥50% wound healing at year five.
results.detail: Long-term healing supports durability, but does not establish continuously healed, blister-free skin for at least three years. No molecular analysis demonstrates maintenance by corrected stem-cell clones; biopsies assessing collagen VII stopped after year two.
results.quote:
At year five, 70% (21/30) of treated sites demonstrated ≥ 50% wound healing compared to baseline 
by investigator global assessment.

results.finding: In 7 graft recipients with RDEB, 3 had detectable collagen VII NC2 domain or anchoring fibrils one year after treatment.
results.detail: The FDA label reports protein restoration in treated tissue in a single-arm clinical study, alongside clinical wound-function and safety assessments.
results.quote:
One year after treatment with ZEVASKYN, 3 patients were positive for 
NC2 or AFs.

results.finding: VIITAL enrolled 11 patients with 43 wound pairs; 81% of treated wounds reached ≥50% healing at Month 6.
results.detail: Healing occurred in 35/43 treated versus 7/43 control wounds (p<0.0001), confirmed at least two weeks later. Mean Wong-Baker FACES pain reductions were 3.07 versus 0.90 points (p=0.0002); one control wound lacked a baseline pain value.

results.finding: FDA approved ZEVASKYN in 2025 for wounds in adult and pediatric RDEB patients; approval covers one genetic disease.
results.detail: The approved product comprises autologous cellular sheets genetically modified ex vivo with functional COL7A1 to express collagen VII. A sample size is not applicable to the licensing decision.
results.quote: Initial U.S. Approval:  2025

results.finding: Hologene 5 enrolled 2 participants; 0 were evaluable for the 12-month transplantation-success endpoint.
results.detail: The uncontrolled trial ended prematurely. Its endpoint differed from the required 24-week healing and pain comparisons; no statistical analysis was performed.
results.quote: The primary endpoint could not be evaluated in any subject.

results.finding: FDA licensed ZEVASKYN for adult and pediatric RDEB wounds as a 41 cm² autologous cell sheet expressing type VII collagen; patient sample size not reported.
results.detail: The approval authorizes manufacture of prademagene zamikeracel and the LZRSE-Col7A1 retroviral vector. The letter reports licensing, without clinical efficacy or durability results.
results.quote:
Under this license, you are authorized to manufacture the product prademagene 
zamikeracel, which is indicated for treatment of wounds in adult and pediatric patients 
with recessive dystrophic epidermolysis bullosa (RDEB).

results.finding: One-time pz-cel grafting in 11 patients with COL7A1 RDEB showed sustained wound-healing efficacy through 5 years.
results.detail: Only four patients reached five-year follow-up. This conference poster does not establish continuous blister-free healing without further corrective treatment or molecular evidence of maintenance by corrected stem-cell clones. The long-term result is not presented as peer-reviewed; the cited journal paper concerns the primary trial.
results.quote:
At months 12, 18, 24, 30 and up 
to Month 60 post-treatment, a 
great proportion of treated 
wounds demonstrated sustained 
efficacy following a one-time 
surgical application of pz-cel.

results.finding: In one LAMB3 junctional EB patient, transgenic skin remained stable and free of clinical blistering at 72 months after gene and stem cell therapy.
results.detail: The study reports long-term clinical stability but provides no integration-site or equivalent molecular evidence that corrected stem-cell clones maintain the epidermis. A single graft application and absence of further corrective treatment are not established.
results.quote: Despite this dysbiosis, transgenic areas remained stable and showed no clinical signs of eczema or blistering.
